why: What a page control has to look like before a browser-evidence run refuses to touch it. An evidence run reads a site; it does not sign anybody in, does not spend money, does not delete anything and does not post in the operator's name. The only thing it has to go on is the wording on the control, the form around it and the address of the page, so each category here is a set of phrasings that has actually appeared on a control of that kind. The order matters and is the order below: a control that says both 'notification' and 'allow' is a notification control, and a recovery link that also says 'sign in' is recovery, because the narrower reading is the one that keeps the run out of an account. Kept as a record so a phrasing found on a new site is a line added here, with its category, rather than a regex edited in the classifier.

categories.name: notification_control
categories.why: A notification prompt leaves state in the operator's browser profile that outlives the run. The plurals are here because the wording Chrome itself shows is 'Allow notifications', which the singular missed — the control was still withheld, as a browser permission, so the ledger recorded the wrong category for the commonest prompt on the web.

categories.name: browser_permission_control
categories.why: Camera, microphone, location and clipboard are the operator's to grant, not an evidence run's.

categories.name: system_ui_download
categories.reason: download or external application control withheld
categories.why: A download or a handoff to another application leaves the page and the browser entirely.

categories.name: mfa_2fa
categories.why: A second factor is a credential; spending one is never evidence gathering.

categories.name: trusted_device
categories.why: Marking a machine trusted changes what the account will accept later, long after the run ends.

categories.name: account_recovery_submission
categories.why: Recovery sends mail and can lock the operator out of his own account. Tested before the sign-in family, because a recovery link usually sits on a sign-in page and says so.

categories.name: authentication_submission
categories.why: An evidence run reads what a signed-out visitor sees; signing in is the operator's act.

categories.name: purchase_subscription_payment
categories.why: Money is the one boundary that always stays with the operator.

categories.name: destructive_confirmation
categories.why: Nothing an evidence run learns is worth a deletion it cannot undo.

categories.name: messaging_submission
categories.why: Anything that leaves the page as a message is published in the operator's name. Tested last: 'send' and 'share' appear as decoration on pages that submit nothing.

flag_categories_why: Facts read off the control itself, which beat wording: a form carrying a password field is a sign-in form whatever its button says.
